abstract: Cell differentiation requires the specific control of gene expression for each cell type. However, the mechanism by which robust developmental outcomes arise from inherently noisy single-cell dynamics remains unclear. To address this question, we performed a formal analysis of longitudinal time series during the commitment and differentiation of giant single cells. We tracked how the discrete expression states of individual genes changed relative to each other. Despite marked variability in timing and trajectories from cell to cell, we identified reproducible temporal motifs and quantified the strength of temporal correlations among early- and late-regulated genes. Notably, a core gene set exhibited the same relative temporal order in establishing stable or transiently stable expression states in most cells. This suggests that a well-defined gene expression program emerges amidst apparent stochasticity. These results support a model in which induction to differentiation proceeds via a cascade of partially concurrent, discrete genetic switching events that collectively produce gradual, continuous shifts in expression at the population level. This framework reconciles apparently stochastic single-cell behavior with reliable developmental outcomes and suggests general principles for the temporal organization of gene regulation during differentiation. Furthermore, it provides analytic tools that can be broadly applied to longitudinal single-cell datasets to design temporally precise interventions in development and disease.
